column4: Its إِنَّهَا عَلَيْهِم مُؤْصَدَةٌ repeats the section's decisive مُؤْصَدَةٌ image almost verbatim: the fire is shut over its people.
Moses sees a distant fire, says آنَسْتُ نَارًا, and hopes to find هُدًى at it; sight, the section's ء ن س sense, fire, and road-guidance meet in one ayah.
Moses says آنَسْتُ نَارًا and offers to return with news or a burning brand so his family may warm themselves, joining distant perception to fire as sheltering utility.
The fire is perceived with ءَانَسَ beside the Mount, then approached for news or a brand for warmth; this is the section's night traveler, high-place fire, sight, and rest scene.
The direction of distant sight is reversed: when the Blaze sees them مِن مَّكَانٍ بَعِيدٍ, they hear its rage; the far-off fire is no welcoming marker but an active threat.
The lamp shines in a niche, its oil almost glowing before fire touches it, and نُّورٌ عَلَىٰ نُورٍ culminates in God's guidance to His light; illumination, fire, and guidance are explicitly joined.
A kindled fire first lights its surroundings, then God removes their نُور and leaves them in darkness unable to see; the guiding function of fire is withdrawn before their eyes.
The threatened حُسْبَانًا مِّنَ السَّمَاءِ is the Quranic wording behind the source section's dictionary gloss “a fire from heaven that burns it,” giving the ح س ب family its destructive-fire sense.

One ayah makes night سَكَنًا and sun and moon حُسْبَانًا; the section's lexicon separately calls a resting fire al-sakan and records destructive fire as a ḥusbān sense, so their ordinary cosmic meanings meet here.
فَإِنْ آنَسْتُم مِّنْهُمْ رُشْدًا is the section's other cited ء ن س formulation: perceiving maturity or right judgment clarifies how آنَسَ can mean discerning rather than social familiarity.
The Creator directly asks whether people have considered the fire they kindle, making ordinary human fire an object of divine interrogation.
God says He made that fire تَذْكِرَةً وَمَتَاعًا: it both points beyond itself and serves its users, matching the section's fire as reminder and useful marker.
The wealth-gatherer يَحْسَبُ أَنَّ مَالَهُ أَخْلَدَهُ; the same “he supposes” stance as 90:5 and 90:7 leads directly into the fire shut over him in 104:8.
The kindled fire تَطَّلِعُ عَلَى الْأَفْئِدَةِ, rising over and reaching hearts; it turns upward-reaching flame into inward enclosure.
The Blaze تَدْعُوا مَنْ أَدْبَرَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ, so the fire itself calls the person who turned away from the right direction.
وَجَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ identifies the one called by the fire in 70:17 as the person who gathered and withheld wealth, matching the section's hoarder-to-fire movement.
فَأَنذَرْتُكُمْ نَارًا تَلَظَّىٰ makes blazing fire itself the announced warning after the surah's divided courses of action.
The person entering that warning-fire is الَّذِي كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ, specifically one who denies and turns away from the guidance set out before it.
وَمَا هُم بِخَارِجِينَ مِنَ النَّارِ states the final consequence of enclosure: there is no exit from the fire.
They wish to leave the fire but وَمَا هُم بِخَارِجِينَ مِنْهَا; this independently repeats the section's exitless, closed-fire claim.
Whenever they try to leave it from anguish they are returned to it, staging repeated failed escape from the enclosing fire.
كُلَّمَا أَرَادُوا أَن يَخْرُجُوا مِنْهَا أُعِيدُوا فِيهَا turns the section's sealed condition into a repeated action: every attempted exit ends inside again.
When Moses reaches the fire, فَلَمَّا أَتَاهَا نُودِيَ يَا مُوسَىٰ; the far-seen marker actually becomes an address, beginning the guidance he hoped to find in 20:10.
At the fire God says He has chosen Moses and commands him to listen to revelation, supplying the concrete guidance anticipated in 20:10.
On reaching the fire Moses is called and those in and around it are blessed; the apparently ordinary warming fire opens into a divine encounter.
When Moses comes to it, he is called from the tree in the blessed valley beside the Mount; the high-place fire proves to be the location of divine direction.
The question أَأَنتُمْ أَنشَأْتُمْ شَجَرَتَهَا أَمْ نَحْنُ الْمُنشِئُونَ shifts attention from human ignition to God's creation of the fire's tree.
God makes fire for people from the green tree, فَإِذَا أَنتُم مِّنْهُ تُوقِدُونَ; fire's surprising created source makes it a sign rather than merely a human tool.
الَّذِي جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ identifies the possessor whose calculation and accumulation end in the closed fire of 104:8.
كَلَّا لَيُنبَذَنَّ فِي الْحُطَمَةِ overturns the hoarder's expectation by casting him into the Crusher later identified as God's kindled fire.
نَارُ اللَّهِ الْمُوقَدَةُ identifies the Crusher of 104:4 and the enclosing subject of 104:8 as God's kindled fire.
فِي عَمَدٍ مُّمَدَّدَةٍ completes the مُؤْصَدَةٌ scene with extended columns, giving structural force to the shut enclosure named in 104:8.
كَلَّا إِنَّهَا لَظَىٰ introduces the blazing fire that then strips, calls the one who turned away, and claims the hoarder.
نَزَّاعَةً لِّلشَّوَىٰ gives the Blaze's bodily action before 70:17 makes it call its target; this is punitive flame rather than a distant useful light.
The second course begins with one who is miserly and deems himself self-sufficient, the stance that leads through 92:10 to the warning-fire of 92:14.
His denial of الْحُسْنَىٰ specifies what “turning away” means before 92:14-16 name his fire.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَىٰ makes the rejected course itself a facilitation toward hardship, preparing the fire that marks its end.
وَمَا يُغْنِي عَنْهُ مَالُهُ إِذَا تَرَدَّىٰ joins useless wealth to the fall immediately before divine guidance and the blazing-fire warning.
إِنَّ عَلَيْنَا لَلْهُدَىٰ places God's responsibility for guidance directly before the fire-warning, making warning-fire part of the surah's two-course orientation.
لَا يَصْلَاهَا إِلَّا الْأَشْقَى identifies who enters the fire of 92:14 before 92:16 defines him as the denier who turns away.
Hell's fire has a surrounding pavilion, أَحَاطَ بِهِمْ سُرَادِقُهَا, and is called an evil resting place; it reverses both the open beacon and fire beside which one rests.
Hell is a bed beneath them and coverings above them, لَهُم مِّن جَهَنَّمَ مِهَادٌ وَمِن فَوْقِهِمْ غَوَاشٍ, turning rest and shelter into total fiery confinement.
Layers of fire lie above and below them, and God uses that very scene to make His servants fear; enclosure and warning are one image.
وَإِنَّ جَهَنَّمَ لَمُحِيطَةٌ بِالْكَافِرِينَ states that Hell already encompasses the disbelievers, joining the section's covering sense of disbelief to enclosing punishment.
Punishment covers them from above and from beneath their feet, making the encompassing claim of 29:54 spatially explicit.
أَلَا إِنَّ جَهَنَّمَ لَمُحِيطَةٌ بِالْكَافِرِينَ directly makes encompassing Hell the boundary around those who cover or reject.
They are thrown bound into a ضَيِّقًا, a narrow place of the fire seen from afar in 25:12; the distant threat closes into physical confinement.
God gives one person a light with which he walks among people, while the other remains in darkness لَيْسَ بِخَارِجٍ مِّنْهَا; guiding light and exitless enclosure are set against each other.
God brings believers from darkness into light, while false patrons bring their followers from light into darkness and on to abiding in the Fire; direction is reversed into confinement.
Believers' light runs before them and on their right as they move toward their promised destination, an eschatological light that visibly guides its travelers.
Hypocrites ask to take light from believers, then a wall with a gate divides inward mercy from outward punishment; sought light becomes an impassable boundary.
The people outside the wall are told that false hopes deceived them until God's command came; this gives the self-deception behind their loss of guiding light.
After the wall closes the division, their refuge is the Fire and no ransom is accepted, completing the movement from borrowed-light plea to inescapable destination.

God guides those who seek His pleasure to paths of peace, brings them from darkness into light, and guides them to a straight path; light and routes perform the same guiding work as the section's beacon.
Revelation is made نُورًا نَّهْدِي بِهِ, a light by which God guides; this states in nonmaterial terms the exact light-guidance relation embodied by the road fire.
God makes the stars so people may be guided by them in the darknesses of land and sea, the Quran's clearest parallel to a night traveler steering by a distant elevated light.
God places roads in the earth لَعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُونَ; the road itself is furnished for guidance just before signs and stars are named.
وَعَلَامَاتٍ وَبِالنَّجْمِ هُمْ يَهْتَدُونَ joins road-marks and a high distant light as means of finding the way, closely matching the section's manār.
God makes سُبُلًا لَّعَلَّكُمْ تَهْتَدُونَ in the earth; it directly states the section's claim that the laid-out route serves guidance.
Mountain passes are made as roads لَّعَلَّهُمْ يَهْتَدُونَ, joining elevated terrain, a traversable way, and guidance.
The rhetorical question asks who guides people through the darknesses of land and sea, placing guidance precisely in the travel-darkness where the section's fire appears.
لَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ is what the garden owner should have acknowledged before the threatened ḥusbān; it directly corrects the 90:5 supposition that no one has power over him.
The man's fruit is encompassed and he wrings his hands over what he spent after the threatened ḥusbān, showing the ruin produced by the source section's “fire from heaven” gloss.
He has no party to help him apart from God and cannot defend himself, answering the delusion of secure power that precedes the section's enclosing fire.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God's way are warned of painful punishment, supplying the moral cause of the fire scene in 9:35.
Hoarded treasure is heated in Hell's fire and brands foreheads, sides, and backs; accumulated wealth itself becomes the instrument of fire.
مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُ وَمَا كَسَبَ denies that wealth and gain can protect their owner immediately before his flaming fire.
سَيَصْلَىٰ نَارًا ذَاتَ لَهَبٍ gives the fire consequence for the man whose wealth cannot avail him in 111:2.
Those who consume orphan wealth unjustly consume only fire into their bellies; misuse of wealth owed to the vulnerable is made fire before the final judgment.
ثُمَّ الْجَحِيمَ صَلُّوهُ orders the condemned into Hell between the failure of wealth in 69:28 and the failure to urge feeding the poor in 69:34.
وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ names refusal to promote feeding the poor as a cause of the fire sentence in 69:31, linking that fire to the unchosen ascent of surah 90.
The people of Saqar confess وَكَانَ لَا نُطْعِمُ الْمِسْكِينَ; failure to feed the needy is explicitly one road into the fire named in 74:42.
The ayah opens with God's guidance and ends with Hell as the abode of those gathered blind, dumb, and deaf; failed sight and failed guidance terminate in fire.
Many destined for Hell have eyes with which they do not see; this makes refusal or failure to perceive the available sign a concrete antecedent of fire.
Hell is displayed openly to the disbelievers, reversing the hidden or unperceived fire before 18:101 explains the covering over their eyes.
Their eyes had been فِي غِطَاءٍ عَن ذِكْرِي and they could not hear; a covering over perception explains why the warning displayed in 18:100 had not guided them.
Those who submit تَحَرَّوْا رَشَدًا, deliberately seek right direction; this is the successful counterpart to the travelers who follow the guiding sign.
The deviators become firewood for Hell, so the immediately preceding search for right direction divides from becoming fuel for fire.
Travel through the land should produce hearts that understand and ears that hear; the true blindness is in hearts, joining journey, perception, and the heart reached by fire in 104:7.
Whoever follows God's guidance will neither go astray nor suffer, stating the safe course whose concrete emblem in 20:10 was the distant fire.
Turning away from God's reminder yields constricted life and resurrection blind, reversing both the useful reminder-fire and the sight by which it is followed.
The resurrected person asks why he has been raised blind although he once saw, foregrounding the failed use and eventual loss of sight.
God answers that His signs came but were forgotten, so the person is forgotten that Day; ignored guidance explains the blindness of 20:124-125.
One who opposes the messenger after guidance is clear and follows another way is left to that choice and burned in Hell; route, following, rejected guidance, and fire form a single causal chain.
The inhabitants of the Blaze say that if they had listened or reasoned they would not be among its companions; unheeded direction is what changed warning into punishment.
The divine question asking whether Moses' report has reached the addressee frames the fire scene as a transmitted reminder; 20:10 supplies the fire itself.
The garden owner boasts of greater wealth and followers; this is the wealth-based confidence that the threatened ḥusbān of 18:40 will expose.
He enters his garden wronging himself and assumes it will never perish, a concrete false estimate immediately upstream of the destructive sky-sent ḥusbān.
His companion asks أَكَفَرْتَ بِالَّذِي خَلَقَكَ, naming disbelief toward the Creator within the very passage where the ḥusbān destroys presumed security.
مَا أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّي مَالِيَهْ is the condemned person's admission that wealth failed, and 69:31 then orders him into Hell.
ثُمَّ أَدْبَرَ وَاسْتَكْبَرَ supplies another person who turns his back before 74:26 announces Saqar, paralleling the one called by the Blaze in 70:17.
سَأُصْلِيهِ سَقَرَ gives the fire consequence of the turning and arrogance in 74:23.
The question مَا سَلَكَكُمْ فِي سَقَرَ asks what course brought them into Saqar; 74:44 answers with failure to feed the needy.
A fiery whirlwind strikes an aged person's fruit garden and burns it, a concrete Quranic parallel to destructive fire arriving upon cultivated security.
Hell answers God's question whether it is full by asking for more; like the calling Blaze of 70:17, fire is given a voice rather than remaining a passive destination.
إِنَّهَا لَإِحْدَى الْكُبَرِ identifies Saqar as one of the greatest signs before 74:36 calls it a warning.
نَذِيرًا لِّلْبَشَرِ makes the fire passage itself a warning to humanity, parallel to fire as تَذْكِرَة in 56:73.
God makes night for rest, لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ, and day for sight; the section's “resting fire” stands at the junction of those two ordinary functions.
Night is made so people may rest in it and day is made giving sight, pairing س ك ن with visibility in the same contrast that the night fire resolves.
God appoints night for rest and day for seeing; a fire that offers both repose and visibility becomes a compact meeting of the two gifts.
If God made night continuous, no deity could bring light; the question exposes how indispensable a visible light is within travel-darkness.
If day were continuous, no deity could bring night لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ; rest belongs to darkness even as the section's fire makes that darkness traversable.
Night is for rest and day for seeking bounty so that people may give thanks, completing the ordered alternation behind 28:71-72.
وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَىٰ depicts night actively covering, directly illustrating the source section's statement that night “covers with its darkness.”
وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَاهَا makes night cover the sun, a concrete Quranic formulation of darkness hiding the light seen by a traveler.
يُغْشِي اللَّيْلَ النَّهَارَ describes God covering day with night, supplying the actual covering action behind the source section's figurative k-f-r account of night.
يُكَوِّرُ اللَّيْلَ عَلَى النَّهَارِ wraps night over day; darkness is pictured as a covering laid upon light.
God effaces the sign of night and makes the sign of day visible, distinguishing obscuring darkness from the light by which people seek their way and livelihood.
When daylight is stripped from night, people are suddenly in darkness; the scene isolates loss of illumination like the extinguished fire-light in 2:17.
Layered darkness leaves a person barely able to see his own hand, and whoever receives no نُور from God has no light; it is the full absence of the section's guiding illumination.
The sun is radiance and the moon نُور, with measured stations for knowing years and حساب; illumination and the ح س ب field meet here in ordered reckoning rather than destructive ḥusbān.
الشَّمْسُ وَالْقَمَرُ بِحُسْبَانٍ uses the ح س ب family for precise celestial measure, a meaningful counter-sense to the source section's sky-sent destructive ḥusbān.
Those who reject wish to extinguish God's نُور with their mouths, but God completes it; guiding light is treated as a flame opponents cannot put out.
The repeated attempt to extinguish God's light and God's completion of it makes illumination an irrepressible guide despite rejection.
The blind and the seeing are declared unequal, setting the perceptual boundary presupposed by a traveler who can or cannot discern the fire.
Darknesses and light are declared unequal, the basic boundary reversed when a fire first illuminates and then becomes closed punishment.
Shade and scorching heat are declared unequal; the useful sheltering side of fire cannot be confused with punitive burning.
The ayah asks whether blind and seeing, or darknesses and light, can be equal, then challenges false creators; perception, illumination, and the true Creator are held together.
The nearest heaven's مَصَابِيح beautify it but are also made missiles against devils; an elevated light carries both visible-marker and punitive functions.
God commands the fire to be coolness and safety for Abraham; fire that would imprison and burn becomes, by divine speech, a place of rescue.
Believers are commanded to protect themselves and their families from a fire guarded by stern angels; this supplies the punitive pole beside the light of 66:8.
The repentant move with their light before and beside them and ask God to perfect it, while 66:6 has just warned of fire; one divine illumination guides where the other fate burns.
After their fire-light is removed in 2:17, they are deaf, dumb, and blind and do not return; the sensory loss fixes their inability to retrace the route.
Their garments are pitch and fire covers their faces, تَغْشَىٰ وُجُوهَهُمُ النَّارُ; flame becomes an adhering cover rather than a visible point ahead.
Garments of fire are cut for the disputants, turning fire into clothing that surrounds the body instead of a beacon outside it.
The servants ask their Lord to turn Hell's punishment away because its torment is inseparable; prayer marks the boundary before fire becomes one's abode.
Hell is an evil مُسْتَقَرًّا وَمُقَامًا, reversing the source section's secondary idea of fire as something beside which one rests.
Hell is brought forward and the human being finally remembers; the warning once available at a distance becomes present when remembrance is too late.
The declaration that human efforts are diverse introduces the two opposed courses whose second end is the blazing fire of 92:14.
Giving and being mindful of God begin the successful course, the specific behavioral opposite of the miserly self-sufficiency that leads toward the warning-fire.
Affirming the finest promise is the opposite response to the denial in 92:9 and 92:16, marking the fork before fire.
God eases the giver toward ease, the other destination set against being eased toward hardship and warned of flame.
Abraham's people propose burning him, but God saves him from the fire; one ayah turns intended fiery confinement into rescue and a sign.
The persecutors command one another to burn Abraham and support their gods, supplying the human punitive intention that God's command to the fire reverses in 21:69.
God makes night a garment and sleep repose, then makes day a rising; covering darkness and rest meet in one formulation behind the section's night-side fire.
Faces are covered as if by pieces of dark night and their owners are companions of the Fire, joining night as covering directly to fiery confinement.
The Book brings people from darknesses into light by God's permission and onto His path, explicitly joining illumination to route-guidance.
A light and clarifying Book are said to have come from God; 5:16 then states that God guides by it along paths of peace.
God guides the human being to the way, leaving a grateful or ungrateful response; the next ayah gives the ungrateful response its fire consequence.
Chains, shackles, and a Blaze are prepared for the ungrateful, turning rejection of the shown way in 76:3 into both enclosure and fire.
Each group thrown into Hell is asked by its keepers whether a warner came, making ignored warning the immediate issue inside the fire scene.
They admit that a warner came but they denied him, supplying the rejected guidance behind their acknowledgment in 67:10.
The أصحاب الأخدود are identified by a fire full of fuel, establishing the trench-fire witnessed in the following ayat.
The persecutors sit over the fuel-filled fire, a spatial reversal of fire closing over its inhabitants.
They witness what they do to the believers, placing culpable human sight beside the fire and sharply answering the supposition that no one sees.
Wealth and children cannot avail the disbelievers against God, and they become fuel for the Fire; presumed protection becomes the material of punishment.
Disbelievers spend wealth to block God's way, then suffer regret, defeat, and gathering into Hell; wealth used against the path ends in fire.
Neither wealth nor children avail their owners against God, and those owners are companions of the Fire, repeating the wealth-to-fire reversal.
The command to seize and shackle the condemned person begins the physical enclosure that continues through Hell in 69:31 and the long chain in 69:32.
The command to bind him in a chain of seventy cubits gives structural force to the confinement surrounding the fire sentence.
The people of Saqar confess that they denied the Day of Judgment, another precise form of the denial that turns a warning into fire.
Failure to urge feeding the poor is named before Hell is brought forward in 89:23, tying the visible fire to refusal of surah 90's ascent.
Consuming inheritance greedily adds a concrete misuse of property to the conduct judged when Hell is brought near.
Excessive love of wealth completes the wealth-centered failure immediately before the judgment scene and the brought-near Hell.
After Hell is brought forward, no one punishes as God punishes; this reverses the human supposition that no one has power over him.
No one binds as God binds, giving the enclosing consequence of the false confidence answered in 89:25.
“Does he not know that God sees?” directly answers the arrogant supposition that no one sees, making divine sight the warning before seizure.
At the reached fire God identifies Himself and commands worship and prayer for remembrance, giving concrete content to the guidance Moses hoped to find there.
The voice at the fire identifies its speaker as God, the Mighty and Wise, completing the transition from a perceived roadside fire to revelation.
Faces are turned about in the Fire while its people wish they had obeyed God and the Messenger; rejected direction becomes bodily exposure to flame.
They say they obeyed leaders who led them away from the path, supplying the misdirection whose fire consequence appears in 33:66.
The people in punishment ask their Lord to bring them out and promise not to return to wrongdoing, directly voicing a desired exit.
God orders them to remain despised in it and not speak, closing the requested exit of 23:107.
Hell has seven gates with an apportioned group for each, giving the punitive destination an explicit bounded architecture.
The addressees will surely see Hellfire, reversing the earlier failure to perceive the warning before it becomes punishment.
They will see it with the eye of certainty, making unavoidable direct sight the final counterpart to a distant sign that could once be followed.
When they see the promised punishment brought near, the disbelievers' faces are distressed; what was treated as remote becomes an immediate visible threat.
Transgression begins the course whose destination is identified as Hell in 79:39.
Preferring the nearer life specifies the choice that makes Hell the refuge in the next ayah.
Hell is the refuge for the one who transgressed and preferred the nearer life, turning a chosen orientation into a final dwelling.
The voice at the reached fire identifies the sacred valley of Tuwa, showing that the distant fire has led Moses to a marked sacred place.
The garden owner doubts the Hour and expects an even better return, extending the false estimate that the sky-sent ḥusbān overturns.
Night is made a garment, another compact Quranic statement of the darkness that covers what the road traveler must discern.
Moses is commanded to bring his people from darknesses into light and remind them of God's days, joining his mission to illumination and remembrance.
God sends clear signs to bring people from darknesses into light, restating the directional work performed by illumination.
One whose breast God opens is upon light from his Lord, while hard hearts are in manifest error; received light and refusal divide into opposed conditions.
A piercing flame pursues the one who snatches a hearing, giving an elevated visible flame a punitive rather than guiding function.
God commands that every stubborn disbeliever be cast into Hell, beginning a short judgment scene whose next ayah names refusal of good.
The person cast into Hell is a preventer of good, linking the fire sentence to obstruction of the good course.
The disbelievers are told to enter Hell's gates and remain there, making the gate a one-way boundary into lasting abode.
The criminals remain perpetually in Hell's punishment, another formulation of the section's exitless closure.
The punishment is not lightened and they are left in despair, specifying the unrelieved condition of the confinement in 43:74.
The disbelievers' fire neither ends in death nor is lightened, making the closed destination temporally as well as spatially inescapable.
